L07 · Definite Matrices & SVD

L07 · Definite Matrices & the Singular Value Decomposition

Lecture 7 (slides "Singular Value Decomposition", 20 pages) · Deisenroth §3.2.3 and Ch. 4.5–4.6 · Strang Ch. 7

Lecture 7 slides (PDF) Revision notes: SVD via a flat-to-3D filter Problem Set 7 (P1–P4, P9, P11–P13 SVD) with solutions Read them all on this page ↓

The eigen-decomposition of L06 needs a square matrix, and works best when the matrix is symmetric. The singular value decomposition (SVD) works for every matrix, of any shape. In order, this lecture covers: positive and negative (semi-)definite matrices, with their "angle" picture and the eigenvalue test; why A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are always positive semi-definite; the SVD A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ and the shape of Σ\SigmaΣ; how to compute it from A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A; its geometry (rotate, stretch, rotate: a circle becomes an ellipse); the rank as the number of non-zero singular values, and how to estimate the rank of noisy data; and the rank-kkk approximation used for compression.

Intuition: The lifting filter (revision notes)

A graphics program lifts a flat picture onto a tilted sheet in 3D: a pixel x∈R2x\in\mathbb R^2x∈R2 goes to Ax∈R3Ax\in\mathbb R^3Ax∈R3 with
A=[1−0.80110].A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-0.8\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.A=​101​−0.810​​.
Every output satisfies y3=y1+0.8 y2y_3=y_1+0.8\,y_2y3​=y1​+0.8y2​, so the picture lands on a flat sheet, and a round logo becomes a tilted oval on that sheet. We cannot describe AAA with eigenvectors — Aq=λqAq=\lambda qAq=λq is meaningless when q∈R2q\in\mathbb R^2q∈R2 and Aq∈R3Aq\in\mathbb R^3Aq∈R3. The SVD fixes this by allowing different special directions on the input side (vi∈R2v_i\in\mathbb R^2vi​∈R2) and on the output side (ui∈R3u_i\in\mathbb R^3ui​∈R3), with Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​. It is exactly the matrix the slides use for their geometric example.

#1. Positive and negative (semi-)definite matrices

🧩Background you needquadratic forms — a single number from a vector and a matrix

For a square A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n and x∈Rnx\in\mathbb R^nx∈Rn, the number
x⊤Ax=x⋅(Ax)x^\top Ax=x\cdot(Ax)x⊤Ax=x⋅(Ax)
is a quadratic form: a 1×n1\times n1×n row times an n×nn\times nn×n matrix times an n×1n\times1n×1 column, so the result is 1×11\times11×1. Written out for n=2n=2n=2,
[x1x2][abbd][x1x2]=ax12+2b x1x2+d x22.\begin{bmatrix}x_1&x_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}=ax_1^2+2b\,x_1x_2+d\,x_2^2 .[x1​​x2​​][ab​bd​][x1​x2​​]=ax12​+2bx1​x2​+dx22​.
Every term has degree two, hence "quadratic". Example: with a=2a=2a=2, b=1b=1b=1, d=2d=2d=2 and x=(1,−1)x=(1,-1)x=(1,−1), the value is 2−2+2=22-2+2=22−2+2=2.

Definition: Definiteness

For A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n:

condition, for all xxx name
x⊤Ax≥0x^\top Ax\ge0x⊤Ax≥0 positive semi-definite (PSD)
x⊤Ax>0x^\top Ax>0x⊤Ax>0 for x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0 positive definite (PD)
x⊤Ax≤0x^\top Ax\le0x⊤Ax≤0 negative semi-definite (NSD)
x⊤Ax<0x^\top Ax<0x⊤Ax<0 for x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0 negative definite (ND)
takes both signs indefinite

The strict versions must exclude x=0x=\mathbf 0x=0, since 0⊤A0=0\mathbf 0^\top A\mathbf 0=00⊤A0=0 for every matrix. PD is a special case of PSD.

The picture. Let y=Axy=Axy=Ax. Then x⊤Ax=x⊤yx^\top Ax=x^\top yx⊤Ax=x⊤y is the dot product of xxx with its own image, and from L01 a dot product is ≥0\ge0≥0 exactly when the angle between the vectors is at most 90∘90^\circ90∘. So

  • PSD: AAA never turns a vector by more than a right angle; AxAxAx lies in the half-plane on xxx's side, the dashed boundary x⊤Ax=0x^\top Ax=0x⊤Ax=0 included;
  • PD: the angle is strictly less than 90∘90^\circ90∘, so the boundary is excluded;
  • indefinite: some vectors are turned forward and others turned back.
Remember

x⊤Axx^\top Axx⊤Ax is the dot product of xxx with AxAxAx. PSD means AAA never turns any vector by more than 90∘90^\circ90∘; PD means strictly less than 90∘90^\circ90∘.

#2. The eigenvalue test for symmetric matrices

Testing every xxx is impossible, but for a symmetric matrix the eigenvalues decide everything.

The slide's argument (one direction). Suppose AAA is symmetric and PD, and qqq is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ. Taking x=qx=qx=q,
q⊤Aq>0 ⟹ λ q⊤q>0 ⟹ λ ∥q∥22>0 ⟹ λ>0,q^\top Aq>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\,q^\top q>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\,\|q\|_2^2>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda>0 ,q⊤Aq>0 ⟹ λq⊤q>0 ⟹ λ∥q∥22​>0 ⟹ λ>0,
since ∥q∥22>0\|q\|_2^2>0∥q∥22​>0. In the same way, PSD gives λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0, NSD gives λ≤0\lambda\le0λ≤0 and ND gives λ<0\lambda<0λ<0.

🔍Where does this come from?the other direction: all λi>0\lambda_i>0λi​>0 makes AAA PD

Write A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ (the spectral theorem, L06) and set c=Q⊤xc=Q^\top xc=Q⊤x, the coordinates of xxx in the eigenvector basis. Then
x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=c⊤Λc=∑i=1nλi ci2.x^\top Ax=x^\top Q\Lambda Q^\top x=c^\top\Lambda c=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,c_i^2 .x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=c⊤Λc=i=1∑n​λi​ci2​.
Each ci2≥0c_i^2\ge0ci2​≥0, and c≠0c\neq\mathbf 0c=0 whenever x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0 (because QQQ is invertible). So if every λi>0\lambda_i>0λi​>0, the sum is positive; if every λi≥0\lambda_i\ge0λi​≥0 it is non-negative; and if the signs are mixed, choosing x=qix=q_ix=qi​ for a positive and a negative λi\lambda_iλi​ gives both signs.

Theorem / Key result: Definiteness from eigenvalues (symmetric AAA)

PD  ⟺  all λi>0,PSD  ⟺  all λi≥0,ND  ⟺  all λi<0,NSD  ⟺  all λi≤0,\text{PD}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i>0,\qquad\text{PSD}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i\ge0,\qquad\text{ND}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i<0,\qquad\text{NSD}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i\le0,PD⟺all λi​>0,PSD⟺all λi​≥0,ND⟺all λi​<0,NSD⟺all λi​≤0,
and AAA is indefinite when the eigenvalues have mixed signs. For a 2×22\times22×2 symmetric matrix, a quick test: det⁡A=λ1λ2\det A=\lambda_1\lambda_2detA=λ1​λ2​ and tr⁡A=λ1+λ2\operatorname{tr}A=\lambda_1+\lambda_2trA=λ1​+λ2​, so

  • det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0 and tr⁡A>0\operatorname{tr}A>0trA>0 ⇒ PD;
  • det⁡A<0\det A<0detA<0 ⇒ indefinite;
  • det⁡A=0\det A=0detA=0 and tr⁡A≥0\operatorname{tr}A\ge0trA≥0 ⇒ PSD but not PD.
Worked example: The three filters of L06 (revision notes)
  • S=[2112]S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}S=[21​12​] has λ=3,1\lambda=3,1λ=3,1: PD. Directly, x⊤Sx=2x12+2x1x2+2x22=x12+x22+(x1+x2)2>0x^\top Sx=2x_1^2+2x_1x_2+2x_2^2=x_1^2+x_2^2+(x_1+x_2)^2>0x⊤Sx=2x12​+2x1​x2​+2x22​=x12​+x22​+(x1​+x2​)2>0 for x≠0x\ne\mathbf 0x=0.
  • F=12[1111]F=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}F=21​[11​11​] has λ=1,0\lambda=1,0λ=1,0: PSD, not PD. Indeed x⊤Fx=12(x1+x2)2x^\top Fx=\tfrac12(x_1+x_2)^2x⊤Fx=21​(x1​+x2​)2 is never negative, but it is 000 at x=(1,−1)x=(1,-1)x=(1,−1), the eigenvector of λ=0\lambda=0λ=0.
  • M=[3220]M=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\2&0\end{bmatrix}M=[32​20​] has λ=4,−1\lambda=4,-1λ=4,−1: indefinite. x=(1,0)x=(1,0)x=(1,0) gives x⊤Mx=3x^\top Mx=3x⊤Mx=3, while x=(1,−2)x=(1,-2)x=(1,−2) gives 3−8+0=−53-8+0=-53−8+0=−5.

Check yourself. Is [1221]\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{bmatrix}[12​21​] positive definite? Its trace is 222 and its determinant is 1−4=−3<01-4=-3<01−4=−3<0, so λ=3,−1\lambda=3,-1λ=3,−1: indefinite, not PD — even though every entry is positive.

Common trap

Positive entries do not make a matrix positive definite (the example just above), and det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0 alone does not either: diag⁡(−1,−1)\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1)diag(−1,−1) has determinant 111 and is negative definite. Use the eigenvalues, or the trace and determinant together for 2×22\times22×2.

Level curves. For a PD matrix the curves x⊤Ax=cx^\top Ax=cx⊤Ax=c are ellipses whose axes lie along the eigenvectors, with half-lengths c/λi\sqrt{c/\lambda_i}c/λi​​; a zero eigenvalue stretches the ellipse into a pair of parallel lines; mixed signs open it into hyperbolas (a saddle). This is the bowl shape behind least squares and ridge regression in L05.

Remember

For symmetric AAA: x⊤Ax=∑iλici2x^\top Ax=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^2x⊤Ax=∑i​λi​ci2​, so the signs of the eigenvalues give the definiteness.

#3. Gram matrices A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are always PSD

Take any A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, square or not. We cannot ask for its eigenvalues, but we can form two square symmetric matrices, A⊤A∈Rn×nA^\top A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}A⊤A∈Rn×n and AA⊤∈Rm×mAA^\top\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}AA⊤∈Rm×m. Their quadratic forms are squared lengths:
x⊤(A⊤A) x=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥22 ≥ 0.x^\top(A^\top A)\,x=(Ax)^\top(Ax)=\|Ax\|_2^2\ \ge\ 0 .x⊤(A⊤A)x=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥22​ ≥ 0.
So A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A "knows" how much AAA stretches every vector xxx. This is the observation the whole SVD rests on — and the answer to the slide's "How? You are fully equipped to show this."

Theorem / Key result: Gram matrices

For every AAA, the matrices A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are symmetric ((A⊤A)⊤=A⊤A(A^\top A)^\top=A^\top A(A⊤A)⊤=A⊤A) and positive semi-definite, so all their eigenvalues are real and ≥0\ge0≥0. Moreover A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is positive definite exactly when the columns of AAA are linearly independent: ∥Ax∥2=0\|Ax\|^2=0∥Ax∥2=0 forces Ax=0Ax=\mathbf 0Ax=0, which for independent columns happens only at x=0x=\mathbf 0x=0.

Worked example: The lifting filter, and a quick count

For the lifting filter,
A⊤A=[101−0.810][1−0.80110]=[2−0.8−0.81.64],A^\top A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\-0.8&1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-0.8\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-0.8\\-0.8&1.64\end{bmatrix},A⊤A=[1−0.8​01​10​]​101​−0.810​​=[2−0.8​−0.81.64​],
which is PD because the two columns of AAA are independent (det⁡=3.28−0.64=2.64>0\det=3.28-0.64=2.64>0det=3.28−0.64=2.64>0, trace 3.64>03.64>03.64>0). The 3×33\times33×3 matrix AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ is only PSD: the output sheet is flat, so one direction of R3\mathbb R^3R3 is never reached.

Check yourself. A∈R5×3A\in\mathbb R^{5\times3}A∈R5×3 has rank 333. Then A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A (3×33\times33×3, rank 333) is PD, while AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ (5×55\times55×5, rank 333) has 5−3=25-3=25−3=2 zero eigenvalues.

Remember

x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0x^\top A^\top Ax=\|Ax\|^2\ge0x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0: Gram matrices are symmetric PSD, so their eigenvalues are ≥0\ge0≥0 and have real square roots — the singular values.

#4. The SVD: A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤

Theorem / Key result: Singular value decomposition

Every A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n can be written
A=U Σ V⊤,A=U\,\Sigma\,V^\top ,A=UΣV⊤,
where

  • U∈Rm×mU\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}U∈Rm×m is orthogonal; its columns uiu_iui​ are the left singular vectors and live in the output space Rm\mathbb R^mRm;
  • V∈Rn×nV\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}V∈Rn×n is orthogonal; its columns viv_ivi​ are the right singular vectors and live in the input space Rn\mathbb R^nRn;
  • Σ∈Rm×n\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}Σ∈Rm×n has the shape of AAA and is zero except on its diagonal, which holds the singular values
    σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σmin⁡(m,n)≥0.\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_{\min(m,n)}\ge0 .σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σmin(m,n)​≥0.
    The SVD always exists, for every matrix — which is why Strang called it the "fundamental theorem of linear algebra".

The shape of Σ\SigmaΣ (slide p10). There are min⁡(m,n)\min(m,n)min(m,n) singular values:

  • m<nm<nm<n (wide AAA): a square diagonal block followed by n−mn-mn−m zero columns;
  • m=nm=nm=n: square and diagonal;
  • m>nm>nm>n (tall AAA): a square diagonal block on top of m−nm-nm−n zero rows.

For the lifting filter (m=3m=3m=3, n=2n=2n=2) the shapes are A⏟3×2=U⏟3×3 Σ⏟3×2 V⊤⏟2×2\underbrace{A}_{3\times2}=\underbrace{U}_{3\times3}\,\underbrace{\Sigma}_{3\times2}\,\underbrace{V^\top}_{2\times2}3×2A​​=3×3U​​3×2Σ​​2×2V⊤​​. Always track the sizes: V⊤V^\topV⊤ acts on inputs in Rn\mathbb R^nRn, Σ\SigmaΣ converts from Rn\mathbb R^nRn to Rm\mathbb R^mRm, and UUU acts on outputs in Rm\mathbb R^mRm.

Theorem / Key result: The one sentence to remember: Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​

Multiply A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ on the right by VVV and use V⊤V=IV^\top V=IV⊤V=I:
AV=UΣ⟹A vi=σi ui(column i).AV=U\Sigma\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad A\,v_i=\sigma_i\,u_i\quad\text{(column }i\text{)} .AV=UΣ⟹Avi​=σi​ui​(column i).
AAA sends each right singular vector viv_ivi​ to the left singular vector uiu_iui​, stretched by σi\sigma_iσi​. Likewise A⊤ui=σiviA^\top u_i=\sigma_iv_iA⊤ui​=σi​vi​.

Compact (thin) form. If only rrr singular values are non-zero, the remaining columns of UUU and VVV only ever multiply zeros, so
A=Ur Σr Vr⊤,(m×r)(r×r)(r×n).A=U_r\,\Sigma_r\,V_r^\top,\qquad (m\times r)(r\times r)(r\times n).A=Ur​Σr​Vr⊤​,(m×r)(r×r)(r×n).

Worked example: Shapes and a diagonal matrix (PSet 7, Problem 1)
📄 Original questionPSet 7 · Problem 1 ↗

Consider A=(3001)A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}A=(30​01​). (a) Give UUU, Σ\SigmaΣ, VVV with A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤. (b) What are the singular values of AAA? Which input direction is stretched more by x↦Axx\mapsto Axx↦Ax?

Worked solution

(a) AAA is diagonal with non-negative, already sorted entries, so U=I2U=I_2U=I2​, Σ=A\Sigma=AΣ=A, V=I2V=I_2V=I2​ works.

(b) The singular values are 333 and 111. The direction (1,0)⊤(1,0)^\top(1,0)⊤ is stretched by 333 and (0,1)⊤(0,1)^\top(0,1)⊤ by 111.

Check yourself. For A∈R5×3A\in\mathbb R^{5\times3}A∈R5×3 the shapes are U:5×5U:5\times5U:5×5, Σ:5×3\Sigma:5\times3Σ:5×3, V⊤:3×3V^\top:3\times3V⊤:3×3; there are 333 singular values and the last 5−3=25-3=25−3=2 rows of Σ\SigmaΣ are zero.

A negative entry. D=diag⁡(3,−2)D=\operatorname{diag}(3,-2)D=diag(3,−2) has singular values 333 and 222, not 333 and −2-2−2: singular values are never negative. The sign moves into UUU:
D=[100−1][3002][1001].D=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.D=[10​0−1​][30​02​][10​01​].

Remember

A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ for every AAA; Σ\SigmaΣ has the shape of AAA, min⁡(m,n)\min(m,n)min(m,n) non-negative singular values in decreasing order, and Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​.

#5. Computing the SVD

The slides' derivation. Substitute A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ into the two Gram matrices and cancel V⊤V=IV^\top V=IV⊤V=I or U⊤U=IU^\top U=IU⊤U=I:
AA⊤=UΣV⊤VΣ⊤U⊤=U (ΣΣ⊤) U⊤,A⊤A=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=V (Σ⊤Σ) V⊤.AA^\top=U\Sigma V^\top V\Sigma^\top U^\top=U\,(\Sigma\Sigma^\top)\,U^\top,\qquad A^\top A=V\Sigma^\top U^\top U\Sigma V^\top=V\,(\Sigma^\top\Sigma)\,V^\top .AA⊤=UΣV⊤VΣ⊤U⊤=U(ΣΣ⊤)U⊤,A⊤A=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=V(Σ⊤Σ)V⊤.
ΣΣ⊤\Sigma\Sigma^\topΣΣ⊤ is m×mm\times mm×m diagonal and Σ⊤Σ\Sigma^\top\SigmaΣ⊤Σ is n×nn\times nn×n diagonal, both holding σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​ (padded with zeros). So these are eigen-decompositions:

  • the left singular vectors (columns of UUU) are eigenvectors of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤;
  • the right singular vectors (columns of VVV) are eigenvectors of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A;
  • σi2=λi\sigma_i^2=\lambda_iσi2​=λi​, the eigenvalues, which are ≥0\ge0≥0 because Gram matrices are PSD (§3). That is why singular values are never negative — the question at the bottom of slide p13.
🔍Where does this come from?why v1v_1v1​ is the direction of largest stretch

Write a unit vector x=∑icivix=\sum_ic_iv_ix=∑i​ci​vi​ in the eigenvector basis of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A, with ∑ici2=1\sum_ic_i^2=1∑i​ci2​=1. Then
∥Ax∥2=x⊤A⊤Ax=∑iλici2,\|Ax\|^2=x^\top A^\top Ax=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^2 ,∥Ax∥2=x⊤A⊤Ax=i∑​λi​ci2​,
a weighted average of the eigenvalues. It is largest when all the weight is on λ1\lambda_1λ1​, i.e. x=v1x=v_1x=v1​, giving ∥Av1∥=λ1=σ1\|Av_1\|=\sqrt{\lambda_1}=\sigma_1∥Av1​∥=λ1​​=σ1​. The best direction perpendicular to v1v_1v1​ is v2v_2v2​, and so on. So σ1=max⁡∥x∥=1∥Ax∥\sigma_1=\max_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|σ1​=max∥x∥=1​∥Ax∥ is the largest stretch AAA can produce.

Definition: The recipe (revision notes)
  1. Form A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and find its eigenvalues λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge0λ1​≥λ2​≥⋯≥0. Then σi=λi\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}σi​=λi​​.
  2. Find orthonormal eigenvectors viv_ivi​: the columns of VVV.
  3. For each σi>0\sigma_i>0σi​>0 set ui=Aviσiu_i=\dfrac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}ui​=σi​Avi​​.
  4. If m>rm>rm>r, complete UUU with unit vectors perpendicular to u1,…,uru_1,\dots,u_ru1​,…,ur​ (they solve A⊤w=0A^\top w=\mathbf 0A⊤w=0).

Sanity checks: ∑iσi2=∥A∥F2\sum_i\sigma_i^2=\|A\|_F^2∑i​σi2​=∥A∥F2​ (sum of squares of all entries); for square AAA, σ1⋯σn=∣det⁡A∣\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n=|\det A|σ1​⋯σn​=∣detA∣.

Common trap: The sign trap

It is tempting to take UUU from a separate eigen-decomposition of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤. Don't: eigenvectors are only defined up to sign, and only one sign of uiu_iui​ satisfies Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​. Get VVV from A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A, then define ui=Avi/σiu_i=Av_i/\sigma_iui​=Avi​/σi​. #6. Geometry: rotate, stretch, rotate

Read Ax=UΣV⊤xAx=U\Sigma V^\top xAx=UΣV⊤x from right to left (slide p15):

  1. V⊤V^\topV⊤ — change of basis in Rn\mathbb R^nRn. It re-describes xxx using the perpendicular directions v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ as axes. Lengths and angles do not change, so a circle stays a circle.
  2. Σ\SigmaΣ — scaling in the new basis. Axis iii is stretched by σi\sigma_iσi​, so the circle becomes an axis-aligned ellipse. This step also changes the dimension from nnn to mmm: if m<nm<nm<n the last n−mn-mn−m coordinates are dropped (the zero columns of Σ\SigmaΣ); if m>nm>nm>n, m−nm-nm−n zero coordinates are appended (the zero rows).
  3. UUU — change of basis in Rm\mathbb R^mRm. The ellipse is rotated onto the output directions u1,…,umu_1,\dots,u_mu1​,…,um​.
Theorem / Key result: Circles become ellipses

The image of the unit circle (ball) under AAA is an ellipse (ellipsoid) with semi-axes σ1u1, σ2u2, …, σrur\sigma_1u_1,\ \sigma_2u_2,\ \dots,\ \sigma_ru_rσ1​u1​, σ2​u2​, …, σr​ur​. The lengths of the axes are the singular values; their directions are the left singular vectors; and σ1\sigma_1σ1​ is the largest stretch AAA can produce.

Why: a unit x=∑icivix=\sum_ic_iv_ix=∑i​ci​vi​ goes to Ax=∑iσiciuiAx=\sum_i\sigma_ic_iu_iAx=∑i​σi​ci​ui​, and the uiu_iui​ are perpendicular, so the coordinate along uiu_iui​ is σici\sigma_ic_iσi​ci​, at most σi\sigma_iσi​ (reached at x=vix=v_ix=vi​).

#7. Rank, and estimating the rank of noisy data

Theorem / Key result: Rank from the SVD

The rank of AAA equals the number of non-zero singular values.

Why: UUU and V⊤V^\topV⊤ are invertible and multiplying by an invertible matrix does not change the rank, so rank⁡A=rank⁡Σ\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}\SigmarankA=rankΣ, the number of non-zero diagonal entries. (The slide's argument: rank⁡A⊤A=rank⁡A\operatorname{rank}A^\top A=\operatorname{rank}ArankA⊤A=rankA, and the rank of the symmetric matrix A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is its number of non-zero eigenvalues, which are the σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​.)

Common trap

"Rank = number of non-zero eigenvalues" is true for symmetric (diagonalisable) matrices such as A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A, but not for every square matrix: [0100]\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}[00​10​] has rank 111 and both eigenvalues 000. Its singular values are 111 and 000, which count the rank correctly.

Application — the rank of noisy data (slide p18). Stack nnn data points a1,…,an∈Rma_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R^ma1​,…,an​∈Rm as the columns of A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, with n≫mn\gg mn≫m. If the points satisfy linear relations, so that they lie in an rrr-dimensional subspace, then rank⁡A=r\operatorname{rank}A=rrankA=r. But measurements carry noise, so in practice AAA has full rank mmm. The SVD still sees the structure: rrr singular values are large and the rest are close to zero (about the size of the noise). Counting the large ones gives the approximate rank.

Worked example: Eight noisy points on a plane (revision notes)

Eight points in R3\mathbb R^3R3 lie on the plane y3=y1+y2y_3=y_1+y_2y3​=y1​+y2​ (true rank 222), with noise of about 0.050.050.05 in every entry. The singular values of the 3×83\times83×8 data matrix are
σ1≈5.83,σ2≈2.20,σ3≈0.15.\sigma_1\approx5.83,\qquad\sigma_2\approx2.20,\qquad\sigma_3\approx0.15 .σ1​≈5.83,σ2​≈2.20,σ3​≈0.15.
Two are large and one is tiny, so the approximate rank is 222 — found without being told about the plane. The last left singular vector u3≈(−0.60,−0.54,0.59)u_3\approx(-0.60,-0.54,0.59)u3​≈(−0.60,−0.54,0.59) is almost the plane's normal 13(−1,−1,1)\tfrac1{\sqrt3}(-1,-1,1)3​1​(−1,−1,1): the direction in which the data barely vary. There is no universal cut-off; look for a clear gap (2.20→0.152.20\to0.152.20→0.15 here).

Remember

rank⁡A=#{σi>0}\operatorname{rank}A=\#\{\sigma_i>0\}rankA=#{σi​>0}; with noisy data, count the singular values before the big gap.

#8. Low-rank approximation and compression

A matrix as a sum of layers. Multiplying out UΣV⊤U\Sigma V^\topUΣV⊤ column by column (the outer-product view of L02),
A=UΣV⊤=∑i=1min⁡(m,n)σi uivi⊤=∑i=1rσi uivi⊤.A=U\Sigma V^\top=\sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,n)}\sigma_i\,u_iv_i^\top=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i\,u_iv_i^\top .A=UΣV⊤=i=1∑min(m,n)​σi​ui​vi⊤​=i=1∑r​σi​ui​vi⊤​.
Each layer uivi⊤u_iv_i^\topui​vi⊤​ is an m×nm\times nm×n matrix of rank one (a column times a row) with strength σi\sigma_iσi​. The sum can stop at r=rank⁡Ar=\operatorname{rank}Ar=rankA because the remaining σi\sigma_iσi​ are 000. Keeping only the first kkk layers gives the rank-kkk approximation
A≈Ak=∑i=1kσi uivi⊤=UkΣkVk⊤,rank⁡Ak=k.A\approx A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i\,u_iv_i^\top=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^\top,\qquad\operatorname{rank}A_k=k .A≈Ak​=i=1∑k​σi​ui​vi⊤​=Uk​Σk​Vk⊤​,rankAk​=k.

Theorem / Key result: How good is AkA_kAk​? (Eckart–Young, used without proof)

The error is the sum of the discarded layers, so it is controlled by the discarded singular values:
∥A−Ak∥F2=σk+12+⋯+σr2,∥A−Ak∥2=σk+1 (largest stretch of the error).\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sigma_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\sigma_r^2,\qquad \|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}\ \text{(largest stretch of the error)} .∥A−Ak​∥F2​=σk+12​+⋯+σr2​,∥A−Ak​∥2​=σk+1​ (largest stretch of the error).
No other matrix of rank kkk does better. The fraction of the "energy" kept is
σ12+⋯+σk2σ12+⋯+σr2=∥Ak∥F2∥A∥F2.\frac{\sigma_1^2+\cdots+\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2+\cdots+\sigma_r^2}=\frac{\|A_k\|_F^2}{\|A\|_F^2}.σ12​+⋯+σr2​σ12​+⋯+σk2​​=∥A∥F2​∥Ak​∥F2​​.

Storage. AAA needs mnmnmn numbers. AkA_kAk​ needs kkk vectors ui∈Rmu_i\in\mathbb R^mui​∈Rm, kkk numbers σi\sigma_iσi​ and kkk vectors vi∈Rnv_i\in\mathbb R^nvi​∈Rn:
storage(Ak)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).\text{storage}(A_k)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).storage(Ak​)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).
Increasing kkk never increases the error, but each extra layer costs m+n+1m+n+1m+n+1 more numbers: fidelity against compression.

Geometry of dropping a layer. Dropping σ2u2v2⊤\sigma_2u_2v_2^\topσ2​u2​v2⊤​ removes the short axis of the ellipse: A1A_1A1​ sends the circle to the segment along the long axis, and what is lost is the half-width σ2\sigma_2σ2​. The thinner the ellipse, the better a line approximates it.

P11. Design an SVD-based compression of face photographs: how to arrange the pixels into a matrix, how to choose kkk, and how to judge the result. P12. The design questions in PSet 7 (P11–P12) are answered in words: flatten each face into a row of a data matrix and keep UkU_kUk​, σ1..k\sigma_{1..k}σ1..k​, VkV_kVk​; choose kkk from the cumulative energy ∑i≤kσi2/∑iσi2\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i^2/\sum_i\sigma_i^2∑i≤k​σi2​/∑i​σi2​ and a storage target, not visual quality alone; compare with the relative Frobenius error. For ratings, zeros would be treated as genuine ratings and dominate the decomposition — instead fit a regularised low-rank model only on the observed entries, choose the rank on held-out ratings, and report RMSE (training error alone always falls as the rank grows).

Where this shows up in AI: Where this shows up in AI

Image and video compression; recommender systems (low-rank user × item factors); latent semantic analysis of word–document matrices; denoising (drop the small singular values); the pseudo-inverse A+=VΣ+U⊤A^+=V\Sigma^+U^\topA+=VΣ+U⊤ behind least squares; and PCA in L08, which is the SVD of the centred data matrix.

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, -0.8], [0, 1], [1, 0]])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)          # U: 3x3, s: 2 values, Vt: 2x2
print(s)                             # [1.6248 1.    ]
A1 = s[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0]) # rank-1 approximation
print(np.linalg.norm(A - A1, 2))     # 1.0 = sigma_2

SVD versus EVD. The EVD needs a square matrix and may need complex numbers; its eigenvectors need not be perpendicular. The SVD exists for every real matrix of any shape, always has real orthogonal UUU and VVV, and non-negative σi\sigma_iσi​. For symmetric matrices the two agree up to signs: σi=∣λi∣\sigma_i=|\lambda_i|σi​=∣λi​∣.
